en: The Sutra on the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha’s Mother, translated by the Song dynasty śramaṇa Huijian.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, traveling along the banks of the Monkey River.

In the Kūṭāgāra Hall, the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī—the mother of the Buddha—was then residing in the city of Vaiśālī together with five hundred female *kṣatriyās*, all of whom were Arhats. They had attained the six supernormal powers and mastery of the four bases of psychic power, and their spiritual radiance was majestic and sublime. Their vihāra was located in the royal garden; they had brought immeasurable beings to liberation and had deeply entered the Samādhi of Universal Wisdom. On the day when they beheld that the World-Honored One, along with Ānanda, Śāriputra, and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, had finished their work of conversion and were about to enter parinirvāṇa, she thought: "I cannot bear to see the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and the various Arhats enter *nirvāṇa*. I shall first bring my spirit to rest and return to the original non-being."
The Buddha, possessing all-encompassing wisdom, clearly perceived this and immediately addressed Ānanda:
"Mahāprajāpatī has thought:
'I cannot bear to see the World-Honored One and the Arhats enter parinirvāṇa; I wish to attain extinction first.'"
Upon hearing these instructions, Ānanda immediately prostrated himself and said:
“Now that I have heard your command, my four limbs feel as if they are withering away, my mind is stifled, and my wisdom is exhausted; I do not even recognize the names of the four directions.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Do you think that when Mahāprajāpatī passes into parinirvāṇa, she takes with her the seed of morality, the seed of wisdom, the seed of concentration, the seed of liberation, and the seed of the knowledge and vision of liberation; or the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path?"
He replied, “No.
It was only that the Great Queen passed away seven days after the Buddha’s birth; her maternal compassion was so profound that her great grace remains with the Buddha.”
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"It is just as you have said; indeed, my mother has bestowed upon me the profound kindness of nursing me with her milk, yet I too have an incalculable debt of gratitude toward her."

By virtue of my clear attainment of taking refuge in the Buddha, taking refuge in the Dharma, and taking refuge in the Noble Sangha; by personally practicing the path to the extinction of suffering and the flourishing of illumination; by being without doubt regarding the Triple Gem; and by the complete liberation through the clarity of the eye of wisdom regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—my fetters are untied, and I have attained non-attachment.

If a person can awaken from the delusions of the ignorant and lead them into the true and correct path, causing them to take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of Noble Ones, and personally take refuge in those who have exhausted the path of habitual tendencies—such a disciple of the Way, even if they were to offer all the famous treasures in the world and provide sustenance to their teacher throughout their entire lifespan, would not equal one ten-thousandth of the merit; for taking refuge in the Three Honored Ones brings grace greater than Mount Sumeru, while the disciple remains as small as a mustard seed.
"Therefore, Ānanda, I have bestowed a profound kindness upon Mahāprajāpatī; it is immeasurable.

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī, together with five hundred *śrāmaṇerīs*, arrived at the place where the Buddha was. They all bowed their heads to the Buddha’s feet, then withdrew and stood with palms joined.
Mahāprajāpatī said to the Buddha, "I cannot bear to behold the passing into parinirvāṇa of the Buddha and the Arhats; I wish to enter nirvāṇa first.
The Buddha silently gave his consent.
Mahāprajāpatī stroked the Buddha’s feet with her hand and said:

“I shall no longer behold the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Master of the Dharma, the Teacher of Gods and Men, the Illuminator of the Three Realms; from this day forth, I shall not see him again.”

The five hundred bhikṣuṇīs set forth their words as above, and the Buddha likewise approved of them. For their sake, he expounded upon the afflictions of the body—birth, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and the distress of not obtaining what one desires—as well as the various pure dharmas: the peace of nirvāṇa, which is free from desire, pure, empty, wishless, signless, and extinguished.
All the bhikṣuṇīs were filled with joy; they circumambulated the Buddha three times, prostrated themselves at his feet, and departed.
Returning to the vihāra, they arranged five hundred seats, and each took her place.

Mahāprajāpatī manifested her supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*): she sat down and sank into the earth, then emerged from the east; she transformed herself in mid-air, rising seven tree-heights above the ground. She walked back and forth through the sky, sometimes sitting and sometimes lying down; water issued from her upper body while fire issued from her lower body, and fire issued from her lower body while water issued from her upper body. She again sank into the earth and flew from the east, appearing and disappearing as before, coming from all eight directions and from above and below. She emitted a great radiance to illuminate those in the darkness of the human world and shone upon the various heavens above.
The five hundred *bhikṣus* likewise manifested such transformations and entered *nirvāṇa* simultaneously.
The Buddha said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Tomorrow morning, enter the city and go to the householder Yasa; tell him: [as follows]."

"The Buddha-mother and the five hundred elders have all already entered parinirvāṇa. The Buddha exhorts the householder to prepare five hundred biers, with five hundred portions each of sesame oil, incense, flowers, sandalwood, paulownia, and catalpa wood; and you should provide music and pure sounds as offerings."

Why is this so? Because these *pudgalas* have all attained mastery over the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and have realized the pure concentrations of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apranihita*), and signlessness (*animitta*). Having now attained *nirvāṇa*, they are praised by all Buddhas; a single offering made to them yields immeasurable merit.
Ānanda prostrated himself on the ground and, moved by compassion, respectfully assented. At dawn, he entered the city and went to the gate of the householder’s residence, saying to the gatekeeper:
"Go in and say that I have come."
The gatekeeper entered and reported the matter as it had occurred.

At that time, the householder was on a high terrace amusing himself with musicians; hearing that Ānanda had arrived, his heart was struck with fear and his hair stood on end. He immediately descended from the terrace and went out in haste, prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground. Placing his hands upon his feet, he knelt and said: "Worthy Ānanda!..."
"You have come very early today; this is not your usual custom. What could be the reason for this?
Ānanda, following the Buddha's instructions, explained the matter in detail to the householder.
Upon hearing this, the householder immediately threw himself upon the ground and, raising a great cry of grief, said:
"How could we, who are disciples of the Buddha, have committed such unworthy conduct as to be abandoned by the Śrāvakas, to pass away forever without purpose and without leaving behind any teaching?"
Sighing and sobbing, he spoke again: "Worthy Ānanda!

Since the monastery in Vaiśālī has become entirely empty and silent, we shall no longer see the female mendicant with supernormal powers upon the four royal thoroughfares, walking the public roads of the kingdom as she did in her time of flourishing virtue."
"The royal road has become empty; how profound is this pain! Ānanda replied:

"The Buddha taught that although heaven and earth endure for a long time, they must have an end from their beginning; what flourishes must decline, and those bound by affection must inevitably part. Those who see these anomalies yet seek permanence will soon undergo retribution. The three realms are impermanent, like illusions and dreams. Since ancient times, the suffering of the non-eternal body has brought immeasurable calamity, yet the foolish do not perceive it—they may truly be called blind."

To seek immortality while born in this world, or to meet with others and never part from them, is ultimately impossible. Yet, when those of superior virtue perceive the profundity of the Buddha’s sutras and understand the four marks of impermanence, they are like the blind regaining their sight; through diligent and earnest practice, they may escape heavy suffering.
Ānanda cited several essential teachings to resolve the householder’s doubts; the householder’s mind was liberated and he rejoiced.
Ānanda then went to where the brahmins and householders were gathered. At that time, their assembly was in the lecture hall engaged in a dispute, so he told them:
"The Buddha exhorted the worthy ones to prepare funeral equipment for five hundred people."
"Why is this so? Because the Mother of the Buddha and the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs have all already entered parinirvāṇa.
When the brahmin householder heard Ānanda’s words, there was none among them who did not throw themselves upon the ground, beat their breasts, tear out their hair, and wallow about in lamentation.
"What shall we do? We are left alone and exposed; upon whom shall we rely?
Ānanda spoke again:

"The three realms are an illusion and entirely impermanent; the body is a vessel of suffering, a gathering place for pain. Only Nirvāṇa is peace; therefore, one takes refuge in the Three Honored Ones."
The householder, his mind liberated, bowed his head at [Ānanda’s] feet.
Ānanda returned to where the Buddha was and reported the matter as it had occurred.
The brahmin householder immediately prepared the funeral requisites and hurried to the monastery.
At that time, the garden gate was closed. The householder’s steward sent a man to climb over the wall to open the gate so he might enter the lecture hall.

There were three female śrāmaṇerīs there: one had attained the stage of non-returning (anāgāmin), the next was at the stage of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin), and the youngest was at the stage of stream-entry (srotāpanna).
They said to the steward, “Our teacher is sitting in meditation and has now attained tranquil concentration; be careful not to disturb her.”
He replied, "The Master has already entered parinirvāṇa; he is no longer present.
Upon hearing this, the śrāmaṇera threw himself down and his breath ceased for a moment before he revived, wailing in grief and saying:
"Who will now further instruct us? The holy teachings that severed our bonds have been lost.
When the householders saw this, there was none who did not raise a cry of mourning. Once their lamentation ended, they said to the śrāmaṇera:

"The Buddha originally preached in the sutras that although those bound by affection may meet, they must inevitably part; worldly glory is difficult to preserve, whereas only the Way can endure long. You should simply resolve to strive for the attainment of arhatship and extinguish the suffering of the three realms."
"This is to cast off worldly feelings of grief.
After the householder had completed the cremation, he took the śarīra and went to where the Buddha was. The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Face east, join your palms, and place your right knee on the ground, saying: "

"Those who possess upright faith and upright conduct, who have perfected the three supernormal powers and the six knowledges, and whose spiritual faculties are complete—all of you should come to this assembly. Why is this?
The Mother of the Buddha and five hundred bhikṣuṇīs have now all passed into parinirvāṇa; it is fitting that we gather here."
"It is the same in all four directions.
Thereupon, two hundred and fifty Arhats from each of the four directions flew through the air by means of their supernormal powers and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
The Buddha rose and went to where Mahāprajāpatī Śāriputrī was; a thousand bhikṣus followed him, and they all gathered there.
He said to Ānanda:
"Take the śarīra and place them in the bowl; hold the bowl in my hands.
Ānanda did as he was commanded; he placed the śarīra in the bowl and, kneeling long, presented it to the Buddha. The Buddha received it with both hands and addressed the bhikṣus:

"This gathered relic was originally a defiled body—wicked, foolish, impetuous, and violent; its mind was light and fickle, full of envy, malice, and secret plotting; it was of the kind that ruins the Way, destroys virtue, and acts as a precursor to chaos. Now, my mother has extracted the defilement of a woman’s wicked folly and, practicing the conduct of a man, has attained the path of Arhatship. She has returned to the numinous original non-being, pure as empty space; her practice is lofty and unsurpassed—how truly heroic she is!"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus and the assembly of lay practitioners (gṛhapati):
"Together, build a temple for our mother and the noble nuns (arhantīs).
They all replied: [So be it.]
“Indeed! Thereupon, devas, humans, ghosts, and dragons erected shrines and established banners; they offered flowers and incense and played music, circling the shrine three times.
Those who were moved to grief shook the land as they went to the Buddha with reverent faith, and each time they spoke:
"Birth and death are suffering; there is no peace within the three realms.
With these words he comforted those who had come, and all departed with joy, bowing their heads in reverence.

In the *Sūtra on the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha’s Mother*, it is recorded as a transformation following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa: "One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, my disciples, the śramaṇas, shall be intelligent and wise, no different from me."

Two hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, King Aśoka shall request eight *hù* and four *dǒu* of relics from eight kings, and within a single day, he shall construct eighty-four thousand Buddhist stūpas.
When [the human lifespan] is three hundred years, if there are those who leave the household life to become śramaṇas, they will attain the Way within a single day.
When it is four hundred years, people will frequently recollect the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha of bhikṣus, and will make offerings to their upādhyāyas and ācāryas.
In the fifth century [after the Buddha’s passing], among the śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the common people, there were none who did not weep as they called the Buddha to mind.
In the sixth century, the śramaṇas would go into the mountains, beneath trees, and among burial mounds to seek the Way.

At the age of seven hundred, he traveled to study both internal and external scriptures; when any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas questioned him on matters, there was nothing he did not understand or explain, and he completely defeated the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist sects.
At the age of eight hundred, he again thought of practicing the construction of Buddhist stūpas, quickly followed by the construction of Buddhist shrines.
At the age of nine hundred, he then thought of practicing livelihood, seeking out places of profit and loss.
When he reached the age of one thousand years, he went forth to accompany a king, training him in the arts of war and military arrays; he personally engaged in slaughter and took women as his wives.
This is the transformation record following the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha.
